Equal **masses** in identical vessels give equal **weights**, and for a flat-based
vessel the force on the base is just the weight.
**Step 1 — write the force on the base.**
F = P x A = (hρg)A ✓
**Step 2 — express the height through the mass.** The vessels are identical, of base
area A, so
m = ρ(Ah), giving **h = m/(ρA)** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
F = [m/(ρA)]ρgA
= **mg** ✓
independent of the density altogether.
**Step 4 — conclude.** The masses are equal, so the force is **the same in all three
vessels** ✓
**Why the densest liquid does not win.** It is also the **shallowest**, since the same
mass occupies a smaller volume ✓ The greater density and the smaller depth cancel
exactly in hρg, leaving the weight alone.
**A worked check.** Take m = 1 kg, A = 0·01 m², g = 10:
water, ρ = 1000: h = 0·1 m, P = 1000 N m⁻², F = **10 N** ✓
mercury, ρ = 13600: h = 0·00735 m, P = 1000 N m⁻², F = **10 N** ✓
The same pressure and the same force, despite a thirteenfold difference in density.
**Why the vessel's shape matters here.** Only because it is **cubical**, with vertical
walls ✓ Then the base supports the entire weight. In a **flared** vessel the sloping
walls carry part of it, and F ≠ mg - the **hydrostatic paradox**.
**The hydrostatic paradox, stated.** The force on the base depends only on the
**depth** and the **base area**, not on the total weight of liquid ✓ A narrow tall
vessel can exert a greater force on its base than a wide shallow one holding far more
liquid. Here the vertical walls make the two coincide.
**What would differ between the vessels.** The **depths** - A deepest, C shallowest ✓
and the **pressure at any given depth** below the surface, which is greatest in C. Only
the force on the base is the same.
**Why pressure, not force, is the more fundamental quantity.** P = hρg depends on the
liquid and the depth; the force then follows by multiplying by the area ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Maximum in A** ✗ and **maximum in C** ✗ both suppose one
of the competing factors wins. **Minimum in C** ✗ likewise ✓ The cancellation is exact.
∴ the same in all the vessels.

CV² is twice the **energy** stored in a capacitor, so its dimensions are those of
energy.
**Step 1 — recognise the quantity.**
U = ½CV², so **CV² = 2U** ✓ an energy.
**Step 2 — write the dimensions of energy.**
[E] = **[M L² T⁻²]** ✓
with **A⁰**, since energy involves no electric current.
**Step 3 — confirm by building it up.**
[C] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]
[V] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹], so [V²] = [M² L⁴ T⁻⁶ A⁻²] ✓
[CV²] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²][M² L⁴ T⁻⁶ A⁻²]
= **[M L² T⁻² A⁰]** ✓ exactly as expected.
**Why recognising the quantity is quicker.** Spotting CV² as an energy settles the
answer in one line ✓ Building it from the separate dimensions of C and V takes five
times as long and offers five chances to slip.
**The three equivalent expressions.**
U = ½CV² = **Q²/2C** = **½QV** ✓
All three have the dimensions of energy, and each is convenient in different
circumstances.
**Why A⁰ is worth stating.** Energy is a **mechanical** quantity ✓ The current
dimensions must cancel, and they do - which is a useful check that the derivation is
right. An answer carrying A¹ or A⁻¹ would be wrong on that ground alone.
**Other quantities with these dimensions.** Work, heat, torque, moment of a force, and
**LI²** ✓ The last is the magnetic analogue: ½LI² is the energy in an inductor, exactly
parallel to ½CV².
**A worked instance.** A 100 µF capacitor at 10 V:
CV² = 10⁻⁴ x 100 = **10⁻² J** ✓ so the stored energy is 5 mJ - a joule-sized quantity,
confirming the dimensions.
**Why dimensional analysis is useful here.** It catches errors instantly ✓ If a
derivation produced CV² with units of coulombs or volts, something would be wrong.
**Reading the distractors.** **M L T⁻² A⁻¹** ✗ carries a current dimension and only one
power of length. **M⁰ L T⁻² A⁰** ✗ is an acceleration. **M L⁻³ T A** ✗ matches no
standard quantity ✓
∴ M¹L²T⁻²A⁰.

A rolling body has **translational and rotational** kinetic energy, and for a solid
sphere the total is **7mv²/10**.
**Step 1 — write the two parts.**
translational: **½mv²** ✓
rotational: **½Iω²** ✓
**Step 2 — insert the sphere's moment of inertia and the rolling condition.**
I = **(2/5)mR²** ✓ for a solid sphere about its centre
ω = **v/R** ✓ for rolling without slipping
so
½Iω² = ½(2/5)mR²(v²/R²) = **(1/5)mv²** ✓
**Step 3 — add.**
KE = ½mv² + (1/5)mv²
= (5/10 + 2/10)mv²
= **(7/10)mv²** ✓
**How the energy divides.**
translational: 5/7 = **71%** ✓
rotational: 2/7 = **29%** ✓
so nearly a third of the energy is locked up in the spin.
**Why "without slipping" is essential.** It is what ties ω to v through v = ωR ✓
A sphere skidding down a frictionless slope would have **no** rotation and all its
energy as translation - and would reach the bottom **faster**.
**The general result.** For a rolling body with I = kmR²:
KE = **½mv²(1 + k)** ✓
solid sphere, k = 2/5: **0·7mv²** ✓
solid cylinder, k = 1/2: 0·75mv²
hollow cylinder, k = 1: **mv²** ✓
hollow sphere, k = 2/3: 0·833mv²
**The racing consequence.** Released together down a slope, they finish in order of
**k**: solid sphere first, then solid cylinder, hollow sphere, hollow ring last ✓
The result is independent of mass and radius - only the **distribution** of mass
matters.
**The speed at the bottom.** From mgh = (7/10)mv²:
v = **√(10gh/7)** = 0·845√(2gh) ✓ about 15% slower than a body sliding frictionlessly
down the same height.
**Why friction does no work here.** At the point of contact the rolling body is
**instantaneously at rest** ✓ so static friction, though essential for rolling,
dissipates nothing and energy is conserved.
**Reading the distractors.** **½mv²** ✗ counts only the translation. **(2/5)mv²** ✗ is
the rotational part doubled, and **(5/3)mv²** ✗ matches no body ✓
∴ (7/10)mv².

The orbital period does **not** depend on the satellite's mass.
**Step 1 — equate gravity to the centripetal requirement.**
GMm/R² = mω²R ✓
**Step 2 — cancel the satellite's mass.** It appears on **both** sides:
GM/R² = ω²R ✓
**Step 3 — solve for the period.**
ω² = GM/R³, and T = 2π/ω, so
**T = 2π√(R³/GM)** ✓
with no **m** in it at all.
**Step 4 — conclude.** Both satellites, at the same radius R, have the **same**
period - a ratio of **1 : 1** ✓
**Why the mass cancels.** Gravity supplies a force proportional to m, and the required
centripetal force is also proportional to m ✓ The same cancellation makes all bodies
fall at the same rate - Galileo's result, in orbital dress.
**The familiar consequence.** An astronaut and the space station orbit **together**,
which is why she floats beside it ✓ A spanner released in orbit stays alongside, since
it follows the identical path.
**What the period does depend on.** Only the **central mass M** and the **orbital
radius R** ✓ which is Kepler's third law:
T² = (4π²/GM)R³ ✓ and it is why measuring a moon's period and radius weighs the planet.
**A worked instance.** At R = 7000 km around the Earth:
T = 2π√[(7 x 10⁶)³/(6·67 x 10⁻¹¹ x 6 x 10²⁴)]
= **5830 s ≈ 97 minutes** ✓ for a satellite of any mass whatever.
**Where the mass does matter.** In the **energy** and **momentum**, both proportional
to m ✓
E = −GMm/2R, so the 9m satellite has nine times the binding energy and needs nine
times the fuel to launch - but it orbits in the same time.
**The one caveat.** The derivation assumes m ≪ M ✓ For comparable masses both bodies
orbit their common centre of mass and the period depends on **M + m** - which matters
for binary stars, but not for satellites.
**Why this makes rendezvous possible.** Two spacecraft at the same altitude keep
station automatically ✓ Changing orbit requires changing the **radius**, not the mass -
the basis of all orbital manoeuvring.
**Reading the distractors.** **9 : 1**, **3 : 1** and **1 : 3** ✗ all suppose the
period depends on m ✓ The cancellation in Step 2 forbids it.
∴ 1 : 1.

Capillary rise goes as **1/r**, so a narrower tube lifts the water higher.
**Step 1 — state the formula.**
h = **2S cos θ/(rρg)** ✓
with S the surface tension, θ the contact angle and r the tube's radius.
**Step 2 — see the dependence.**
**h ∝ 1/r** ✓
so halving the radius **doubles** the rise.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The rise is **greater in the tube of smaller diameter** ✓
**Why a narrow tube lifts more.** The upward force is surface tension acting round the
**circumference**, proportional to **r** ✓ while the weight of the column lifted is
proportional to **r²h**. Balancing them leaves h ∝ 1/r.
**A worked instance.** For water, S = 0·072 N m⁻¹, θ ≈ 0:
r = 0·5 mm: h = 2(0·072)/(5 x 10⁻⁴ x 1000 x 9·8) = **2·9 cm** ✓
r = 0·1 mm: **14·7 cm** ✓ five times the rise in a tube five times narrower.
**Why water rises at all.** Its **adhesion** to glass exceeds its **cohesion**, so the
contact angle is near **zero** and the meniscus is **concave** ✓ The curved surface
means the pressure just below it is lower than atmospheric, and the liquid is pushed up
until the deficit is balanced by the column's weight.
**What mercury does instead.** Its contact angle is about **140°**, so cos θ is
**negative** and h comes out negative ✓ Mercury is **depressed** in a capillary - which
is why mercury barometers need a capillary-depression correction.
**Where capillarity matters.**
**plants** drawing water up through xylem ✓
**blotting paper** and towels soaking up liquid ✓
**oil** rising in a lamp wick ✓
**damp** rising in brickwork, which is why a damp-proof course is needed
**Why very fine tubes are needed for large rises.** A rise of a metre needs
r ≈ **15 µm** ✓ comparable with the finest plant capillaries - and even that cannot
account for water reaching the top of a tall tree, which requires transpiration pull as
well.
**The limit of the formula.** It assumes the tube is narrow enough for the meniscus to
be a spherical cap ✓ In a wide tube the surface is flat in the middle and the rise is
negligible.
**Reading the distractors.** **Greater in the larger tube** ✗ inverts the dependence.
**Same in both** ✗ and **independent of diameter** ✗ ignore the 1/r entirely ✓
∴ greater in the tube of smaller diameter.

At constant pressure, **V ∝ T** in kelvin - so doubling the volume doubles the
absolute temperature.
**Step 1 — convert to kelvin.**
27 °C = **300 K** ✓
**Step 2 — apply Charles's law.**
V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ ✓
With V₂ = 2V₁:
T₂ = **600 K** ✓
**Step 3 — find the increase.**
ΔT = 600 − 300 = **300 K** ✓
and since a kelvin and a celsius degree are the same size,
**ΔT = 300 °C** ✓
**Why the kelvin conversion is essential.** Doubling 27 °C would give 54 °C, which is
meaningless ✓ Charles's law holds only on the **absolute** scale, where the volume
extrapolates to zero at 0 K - and that extrapolation is what defines the scale.
**Why the increase and the final temperature differ.**
final temperature: **600 K = 327 °C** ✓ which is the second option
**increase**: **300 K = 300 °C** ✓
Both numbers appear among the options, so reading which is asked for is half the
question.
**A check by the gas law.**
P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, with P constant ✓
V/300 = 2V/T₂, so T₂ = **600 K** ✓
**What the gas does.** It **expands** against the constant external pressure, doing
work
W = PΔV = nRΔT ✓
and the heat supplied is Q = nC_pΔT, part becoming work and part internal energy.
**Why the volume is proportional to T and not to t.** Extrapolating a V-t graph back,
the volume would vanish at **−273·15 °C** ✓ Shifting the origin there turns the
relation into a simple proportionality - which is precisely how the absolute scale was
conceived.
**A worked illustration.** One mole at 300 K occupies 24·9 litres at atmospheric
pressure; at 600 K it occupies **49·8 litres** ✓
**Why a real gas deviates.** Charles's law assumes ideal behaviour ✓ Near condensation
or at very high pressure a real gas departs from it, but at these temperatures air is
very nearly ideal.
**Reading the distractors.** **327 °C** ✗ is the **final** temperature. **600 °C** ✗
treats the celsius reading as absolute, and **54 °C** ✗ doubles 27 ✓
∴ 300°C.

Starting from the mean position, x = A sin ωt; solve for x = A/2.
**Step 1 — write the displacement.**
x = A sin ωt, with ω = 2π/T = **2π/6 = π/3 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — set x = A/2.**
A/2 = A sin(πt/3)
**sin(πt/3) = 0·5** ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
πt/3 = π/6
**t = 0·5 s** ✓
**The landmark worth remembering.** Starting from the mean position, the particle
reaches **half the amplitude** after **T/12** ✓ Here 6/12 = 0·5 s - and the result holds
for any SHM.
**Why so quick a journey.** Near the mean position the particle is moving at its
**fastest**, ωA ✓ so it covers the first half of the amplitude in a twelfth of the
period, while the remaining half takes a further **T/6** - twice as long.
**The timings across a quarter cycle.**
to A/2: **T/12** = 0·5 s ✓
to A/√2: **T/8** = 0·75 s
to A√3/2: **T/6** = 1·0 s
to A: **T/4** = 1·5 s ✓
The particle slows dramatically as it approaches the turning point.
**Why sine and not cosine.** The clock starts at the **mean** position, where x = 0 ✓
sin 0 = 0, so sine is the right function. Starting from an extreme would require
x = A cos ωt - and the answer would be quite different.
**The speed at that moment.**
v = ω√(A² − x²) = (π/3)A√(3)/2 = **0·907A** ✓ still 87% of the maximum ωA = 1·047A.
**The phase angle.** πt/3 = **π/6 = 30°** ✓ a twelfth of the full 2π cycle - which is
the same statement as T/12, read on the reference circle.
**Why the amplitude never appears in the answer.** It cancels from both sides of
A/2 = A sin ωt ✓ The **time** to reach a given **fraction** of the amplitude depends
only on the period.
**Reading the distractors.** **3/4 s** ✗ is the time to A/√2. **3/2 s** ✗ is a full
quarter period, reaching the extreme. **1/4 s** ✗ is half the correct value ✓
∴ 1/2 sec.

Find the phase constant from the displacement at t = 0, then evaluate the total phase at
t = 7·5 s.
**Step 1 — read the wave equation.**
y = 10 sin[(2π/45)t + α] ✓
with amplitude **10 cm** and angular frequency **2π/45 rad s⁻¹**.
**Step 2 — use the condition at t = 0.**
5 = 10 sin α
**sin α = 0·5**, so **α = π/6** ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate the total phase at t = 7·5 s.**
φ = (2π/45)(7·5) + π/6
= 2π(7·5)/45 + π/6
= π/3 + π/6 ✓
**Step 4 — add.**
= 2π/6 + π/6
= 3π/6
= **π/2** ✓
**What the particle is doing then.** sin(π/2) = 1, so
y = **10 cm** ✓ the particle is at its **maximum** displacement, momentarily at rest.
**Why α is π/6 and not 5π/6.** Both have a sine of 0·5 ✓ The question's phrasing takes
the principal value, π/6, which is the standard convention; 5π/6 would describe a
particle at the same displacement but moving the **other** way.
**The period of this wave.**
T = 2π/ω = 2π/(2π/45) = **45 s** ✓ a very slow oscillation.
**Checking the fraction of a cycle.** 7·5 s is **one sixth** of 45 s ✓ so the phase
advances by 2π/6 = **π/3**, and adding the initial π/6 gives π/2 - a quarter of the
way round the cycle from the reference.
**What the phase constant means.** It records **where in its cycle** the particle was
when the clock started ✓ α = 0 would mean starting at the mean position moving
forward; α = π/2 would mean starting at maximum displacement.
**Why the total phase matters.** It fixes the displacement, the velocity and the
acceleration at once ✓
y = A sin φ, v = Aω cos φ, a = −Aω² sin φ ✓
At φ = π/2 the displacement is maximum, the velocity **zero** and the acceleration most
negative.
**A caution about the units.** The phase is in **radians**, and the 2π/45 carries units
of rad s⁻¹ ✓ Mixing degrees and radians is the usual slip in such problems.
∴ π/2.
